faq.a: With a traditional account, you contribute pre-tax dollars, the money grows tax-deferred, and you pay tax when you withdraw it in retirement. With a Roth account, you contribute after-tax dollars, the money grows tax-free, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.
faq.q: What is the difference between Roth and traditional accounts?

faq.a: Roth usually wins when your tax rate in retirement will be higher than your rate today, because you pay tax now at the lower rate. Traditional usually wins when your retirement rate will be lower, because you deduct at today's higher rate and pay later at the lower rate. If the rates are the same, the two come out equal before any other rules are considered.
faq.q: When does Roth win, and when does traditional win?

faq.a: For 2026, the 401(k) elective deferral limit is $24,500, with an $8,000 catch-up for age 50 and over (total $32,500) and an $11,250 catch-up for ages 60 to 63 (total $35,750). The IRA limit is $7,500, with a $1,100 catch-up for age 50 and over (total $8,600). Source: IRS Notice 2025-67, announced November 13, 2025 with news release IR-2025-111.

No. The IRS had not announced the 2027 limits as of November 8, 2026. Milliman projected on October 15, 2026 that the 2027 401(k) deferral limit would be $25,500 with an $8,500 catch-up. That is a projection, not an official figure. No 2027 IRA figure is given here because projectors disagree.
